name: Firestorm Labs
about: Firestorm Labs, based in San Diego, builds Group 2 drones such as the Tempest (under 55 lb, 7-foot wingspan, up to 10 lb payload) and xCell, a drone factory packed into two shipping containers that 3D-prints airframes near the front line, up to 50 drones a month per unit. Holds a $100 million US Air Force contract covering drone delivery, support and R&D. Registered dozens of airframes with the FAA since September 2025.
expected_reason: Sells small military drones to the same buyers as Anduril, Shield AI and AeroVironment.

verdict.what_it_builds: Group 2 drones, including the Tempest (under 55 lb, 7-foot wingspan, up to 10 lb payload), and xCell, a drone factory in two shipping containers that 3D-prints airframes near the front line at up to 50 drones a month per unit.
verdict.buyers: US Air Force, under a $100 million contract covering drone delivery, support and R&D.

overlaps.why: Anduril registers Ghost and Roadrunner aircraft with the FAA and holds large federal awards, so it sells small uncrewed aircraft to the same military buyers Firestorm targets.
Shield AI registers V-Bat aircraft with the FAA and has federal contract awards, which puts it in the same small uncrewed aircraft market for the same buyers.
AeroVironment registers Wildcat and JUMP 20 aircraft with the FAA and holds a large federal contract base, putting it in the same small drone market.
Neros holds Army awards and an IDIQ contract for small drones and is still scaling its factory workforce, so it competes for the same Army drone buys.

verdict.wedge: Containerized, forward-deployed additive production of airframes, up to 50 drones a month per unit, near the front line. The map shows no incumbent doing this.
verdict.reasoning: Firestorm builds Group 2 drones and a containerized factory that prints airframes near the front line, a different production model from most incumbents on the map. Its Tempest competes head-on with Shield AI and AeroVironment, both entrenched in small drones, and with Anduril, which is a portfolio company, so this is a conflict to disclose before any decision. The forward airframe production is the one named wedge, and the $100M Air Force contract and 34 FAA-registered aircraft show real traction. The description gives no unit economics, stage or pricing, so this is a look and not a priority.
open_questions: Is the Air Force $100M contract a ceiling or obligated funding, and what share has been delivered?
How do xCell airframe unit costs and print times compare with the factory output of Anduril, Shield AI and AeroVironment?
Can the Tempest's range, payload and ISR or strike role be shown head-to-head against Shield AI V-Bat and AeroVironment Wildcat?
Is the Anduril portfolio relationship disclosed and handled before any further conversation?
Which of the company's 34 FAA-registered aircraft are in service with the Air Force, and what is the repeat-order rate?
What is the company's funding stage and is it a US small business for SBIR eligibility?

calls.why: DIU's Low Cost ISR call may want small uncrewed aircraft, which Tempest could be; the listing is one line, so the founders should confirm whether it wants air platforms or sensors.
The Air Force topic asks for autonomous drone swarms; Firestorm builds the airframes, but would have to stretch into swarm autonomy and must confirm small business eligibility.

The Army G-BAM topic asks for low-cost, rapidly produced, launched effects at scale, which matches xCell's production model, but the topic is a long-range strike weapon and is pre-release, so the team can talk to its author now and until it opens 2026-12-03.
